shots.src: IMF World Economic Outlook, October 2026 · GDP per capita, PPP, current international $ (PPPPC); 2026+ are IMF estimates and forecasts
shots.narration: Twenty-nine percent. {p} In 2005, the average Hungarian was twenty-nine percent richer than the average Pole, on income adjusted for prices. {pp} In 2011, Poland passed. This year, in the IMF's numbers, Poland is about eighteen percent ahead. {p} And by 2031, in the IMF's forecast, the gap is about the same.

When both countries joined the European Union in 2004, Hungary was the richer one, and it wasn't close. {p} Poland was the bigger country, but the poorer one. {pp} <soft>So what happened? A slow decade, a crisis, and a neighbor that kept growing.</soft>
Quick one before the chart: this is a series about who's passing whom, and Poland keeps showing up. Subscribe so you don't miss the next one. {p} Now, the head start.

shots.src: IMF World Economic Outlook, October 2026 · Hungary's GDP per capita (PPP) as % of Poland's; 2026+ are IMF estimates and forecasts
shots.narration: Here's Hungary as a share of Poland, adjusted for prices. {p} In 1995, a hundred and thirty-three percent. Poland closed some of that in the late nineties. {pp} Then Hungary pulled away again: a hundred and twenty-seven percent in 2004, and a hundred and twenty-nine in 2005. {p} That was the peak.

shots.src: IMF World Economic Outlook, October 2026 · real GDP growth, Hungary (annual %); 2026+ are IMF estimates and forecasts
shots.narration: Here's Hungary's economy, year by year, after inflation. {p} In 2007, it grew a third of a percent. Poland grew almost seven. {pp} Then the 2008 crisis. In late 2008, Hungary needed an emergency loan from the IMF and the European Union, the first EU country to get one in that crisis. {p} In 2009, its economy shrank almost seven percent. Poland's grew two point six. {pp} And in 2012, Hungary shrank again.

shots.src: IMF World Economic Outlook, October 2026 · real GDP growth (NGDP_RPCH, compounded), population (LP)
shots.title: The lost years
shots.narration: Put it together. From 2006 to 2013, after inflation, Hungary's economy actually got smaller, by about two percent. Poland's grew about twenty-seven. {p} That's where the pass happened. {pp} And since then? Hungary barely grew from 2023 to 2025. Poland grew about seven percent. {p} Hungary has about nine and a half million people. Poland has almost four times as many.

shots.src: IMF World Economic Outlook, October 2026 · GDP per capita, current US$ at market exchange rates (NGDPDPC); 2026+ are IMF estimates and forecasts
shots.narration: In plain dollars, at market exchange rates, the race was closer, and it went back and forth for years. {p} In 2023, they were basically tied: about twenty-two thousand dollars a person each. {pp} Since 2024, Poland has been ahead. This year, about thirty-one thousand two hundred dollars, against twenty-seven thousand nine hundred in Hungary. {p} Unlike most countries in this series, Hungary is now behind on both measures.
And if you're enjoying the series, the subscribe button is right there. {p} Now, the four-country race.

shots.src: IMF World Economic Outlook, October 2026 · GDP per capita, PPP, current international $ (PPPPC); 2026+ are IMF estimates and forecasts
shots.narration: Czechia, Hungary, Slovakia and Poland: the Visegrád Four. {p} In 2004, adjusted for prices, Poland was last of the four. Czechia first, Hungary second. {pp} This year, Poland is second, behind only Czechia. Hungary is third, just ahead of Slovakia. {p} Poland went from last to second. Hungary went from second to third.

shots.src: IMF World Economic Outlook, October 2026 · GDP per capita, PPP, current international $ (PPPPC); 2026+ are IMF estimates and forecasts
shots.title: The pass, adjusted for prices
shots.narration: So here's the pass, in the IMF's numbers. {p} In 2010, Hungary was still ahead, by about five hundred dollars per person. {p} In 2011, Poland passed, by about a hundred dollars. For almost a decade, they stayed within a few percent of each other. {pp} Then Poland pulled away. This year, the gap is about nine thousand dollars. And by 2031, in the IMF's forecast, about eleven and a half thousand.

<soft>So, what's your guess?</soft> {pp} Can Hungary close the gap again, {p} or is this the new normal? {pp} Tell me in the comments. {pp} If you're watching from Hungary: {p} does it feel like this where you are? {pp} I read every comment.
And if you missed it, {p} this is the one where Estonia stalled and Poland passed. {pp} It's right here. {pp} I'm Chartbound. {p} See you in the next one.

checks.say: growth 2007: HUN 0.3 (a third of a percent), POL 6.8 (almost seven)
V4 2004: CZE > HUN > SVK > POL (POL last); 2026: CZE > POL > HUN > SVK

yt.title: Hungary Was 29% Richer Than Poland. Now Poland Is 18% Ahead.
yt.description:
Income per person adjusted for prices (IMF World Economic Outlook, October 2026): in 2005 the average Hungarian was 29% ahead of the average Pole. Poland passed in 2011; this year it's ~18% ahead, about the same in the IMF's 2031 forecast. Hungary's slow 2000s (+0.3% in 2007), the 2008 emergency loan, the 2009 recession (−6.8%), 2006–2013 real growth of about −2% vs +27% for Poland, the plain-dollar race, and the Visegrád Four: Poland went from last to second.

Sources: IMF World Economic Outlook, October 2026 (PPPPC, NGDPDPC, NGDP_RPCH, LP). 2026+ figures are IMF estimates and forecasts.
